summary: Defines a metric for the one-way delay of packets across Internet paths. It builds on the IPPM framework in RFC 2330 and makes RFC 2679 obsolete.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7679 defines how to measure the time a packet takes to travel from one host to another. It also explains how to sample measurements and report their uncertainty.

subtitle: Defines how to measure one-way packet delay, collect samples, and report uncertainty.

tldr.problem: Measurements of Internet delay need a shared definition so results can be compared. A round-trip time alone cannot show whether the forward path or the return path is slower.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the delay for one packet, a Poisson-timed stream of measurements, and statistics such as percentiles, median, and minimum.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7679 is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 2679. It also defines how to account for clock and measurement error when reporting results.

today: RFC 7679 is Internet Standard STD 81, published in January 2016. It obsoletes RFC 2679.

sections.title: Why Measure One-Way Delay
sections.content:
RFC 7679 defines a metric for the delay of packets traveling across Internet paths. One-way measurements matter because the forward and return paths may differ, and their queueing or service levels may differ as well.

The RFC separates a singleton measurement, a sample of measurements, and statistics calculated from that sample. Its framework is intended to make results from different measurement implementations comparable.
sections.plainLanguage: A round trip combines two directions that may behave differently. Measuring each direction separately helps identify which path has higher delay.

sections.title: Clocks and Time Differences
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes synchronization, accuracy, resolution, and skew. Synchronization describes how closely two clocks agree; accuracy describes how closely one clock agrees with UTC; resolution is the smallest unit the clock updates; and skew describes how clock agreement changes over time.

For a one-way delay measurement, the source and destination clocks must be synchronized. Accuracy against UTC is not itself needed for the delay difference, but clock resolution and uncertainty in synchronization affect the result.
sections.plainLanguage: The sending and receiving clocks must agree closely enough to compare their timestamps. A clock's smallest update step and changing offset add uncertainty.

sections.title: The Single-Packet Delay Metric
sections.content:
Type-P-One-way-Delay is defined by source and destination IP addresses, a send time, and a maximum waiting time called Tmax. The delay is the time from when the first bit leaves the source to when the last bit reaches the destination.

If the destination does not receive the packet within Tmax, the result is undefined, informally treated as infinite. If duplicate copies arrive, the first non-corrupt copy determines the delay. A packet that is not standard-formed or cannot be reassembled after fragmentation is treated as lost.
sections.plainLanguage: The measurement starts when the packet's first bit leaves and ends when its last bit arrives. If the packet misses the waiting limit, the metric records an undefined result.

sections.title: Measurement Method and Error
sections.content:
A typical method synchronizes the source and destination clocks, timestamps a test packet near sending and receiving, and subtracts the timestamps. Padding used only to reach a target packet size should contain randomized bits so compression on the path does not reduce the measured delay.

The error analysis includes clock synchronization, clock resolution, and the difference between wire time and host time. Calibration should estimate host error under the same measurement load used in the field. The RFC says a calibration bound should place the reported value within the true value plus or minus that bound at least 95% of the time.
sections.plainLanguage: Send a timestamped test packet and compare the sending and receiving times. Calibrate the measurement hosts and report the uncertainty along with the delay.

sections.title: Samples and Delay Statistics
sections.content:
The RFC defines a sample by choosing source, destination, and packet type, then taking measurements at times from a pseudorandom Poisson process between a start and end time. The sample is a sequence of time-and-delay pairs. Poisson sampling is intended to limit bias and avoid self-synchronization; the RFC does not claim that real Internet traffic follows a Poisson process.

The document defines percentile, median, and minimum statistics. Undefined delays count as infinitely large when those statistics are calculated. It also marks the inverse-percentile statistic as deprecated because it had not been used.
sections.plainLanguage: A sample records many one-way delays at selected times. Statistics summarize the sample, and an undefined delay counts as larger than any finite delay.

sections.title: Reporting and Security
sections.content:
Results should include the packet type, the waiting threshold used to distinguish loss from long delay, calibration results, and the path when known. The exact packet type matters because packet protocol, port, size, and treatment can affect the measured value.

Measurements inject packets, so their traffic must remain trivial enough not to cause congestion or distort the result. The RFC also notes that attackers could inject measurement packets or use results for reconnaissance; access to results and control of measurement systems should be guarded.
sections.plainLanguage: Report how the measurement was made so readers can interpret it. Keep test traffic low and protect access to measurement results.
